units.title: Splendid Words
units.subtitle: Rare, long and lovely — for showing off

words.def: the use of irony to mock or show contempt

journey.gloss: to tear flesh like a dog; to sneer

words.story: Sarcasm bites — literally. The Greek verb described dogs tearing at meat, then people biting their lips in rage. Sarcophagus, 'flesh-eater', is a cousin: limestone coffins were said to consume bodies.
words.example: 'Oh, great, more rain,' she said with heavy sarcasm.

words.def: a sentimental longing for the past
words.story: A Swiss medical student, Johannes Hofer, coined it in 1688 for Swiss soldiers abroad who were wasting away from homesickness. It was treated as a real, sometimes fatal, disease.
words.example: The old cartoon filled him with nostalgia.

words.def: someone who claims beliefs they don't live by

journey.gloss: actor; one who plays a part

words.story: In Greek theatre the hypokritēs was simply the actor — the one who 'answered' on stage. Someone wearing a mask in daily life is still an actor, just a dishonest one.
words.example: He preached about saving water, then filled his pool — a hypocrite.

words.def: a foolish person
words.story: In Athens an idiōtēs was a private individual — someone who kept to their own affairs rather than public life. The professional class looked down on such amateurs, and 'layman' slid into 'ignoramus'.
words.example: I felt like an idiot for locking my keys in the car.

words.def: an institution for educating children

journey.gloss: leisure, spare time; what you do with it

words.story: For the Greeks, free time was for thinking, debate and lectures — the noblest use of leisure. So school literally means 'time off'. Tell that to anyone with homework.
words.example: The school bell rang at eight.

words.def: a conference or meeting to discuss a subject

journey.gloss: a drinking party; later, an academic meeting

words.story: A Greek symposium was an after-dinner drinking party with music and conversation — Plato set a famous dialogue at one. Academic conferences kept the name, if not always the wine.
words.example: She presented her paper at an international symposium.

words.def: the earthy smell of rain falling on dry ground

journey.gloss: stone + the fluid in gods' veins

parts.m: the golden blood of the gods

words.story: Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas coined it in the journal Nature for the scent released from rocks and soil when rain falls. They reached for myth: ichor flowed in the veins of Greek gods.
words.example: After the storm, the air was full of petrichor.

words.def: intense enjoyment, interest or eagerness
words.story: To be enthusiastic was to have a god inside you, speaking through you. In the 1700s it was an insult for over-the-top religious zeal — before it became the thing every job ad asks for.
words.example: The puppy greeted us with boundless enthusiasm.

words.def: a protective garment tied over the front of clothes
words.story: Say 'a napron' quickly and it sounds exactly like 'an apron'. Over time, the n hopped from the noun to the article. Its siblings napkin and map (from Latin mappa, a cloth) kept theirs.
words.example: He tied on an apron and started chopping onions.

words.def: an official who enforces the rules of a game

journey.gloss: odd, not equal; a third party

words.story: An umpire is the 'non-peer' — the odd third person called in when two equals disagree. Then 'a noumpere' became 'an oumpere', and the n wandered off.
words.example: The umpire called the ball out.

words.def: a small venomous snake
words.story: Another lost n. German kept it: a viper there is still a Natter. In English the snake slithered out of its first letter.
words.example: An adder basked on the warm path.

words.def: an informal, familiar name
words.story: The opposite of apron: this word gained an n. An 'eke-name' was an extra name — the same eke as in 'eke out' a living, adding a little more.
words.example: Her nickname at school was 'Rocket'.

words.def: a small amphibian with a long tail
words.story: Newt borrowed the n from its article. Its unaltered twin, eft, survives as the name for a young newt.
words.example: We found a newt under the garden stone.

words.def: a small flower with white petals and a yellow centre
words.story: The daisy opens its petals at dawn and closes them at dusk, like an eye waking and sleeping with the sun. Two words got squashed into one.
words.example: She wove a chain of daisies.

words.def: said when parting
words.story: Every goodbye hides a blessing. 'God be with ye' was worn down by centuries of hurried partings, and 'God' became 'good' to match 'good morning' and 'good night'.
words.example: We waved goodbye from the platform.

words.def: a yellow wildflower whose seeds form a fluffy clock
words.story: Look at a dandelion leaf: its deep jagged edges look like rows of fangs. English squashed three French words into one.
words.example: The child blew the dandelion clock into the wind.

words.def: elegant, stylish or upper-class
words.story: No surviving ticket, record or advertisement ever printed 'P.O.S.H.' — the acronym story appeared decades after the word. Its real origin is uncertain; one theory links it to older slang for money.
words.example: They had dinner at a very posh restaurant.

myth.claim: Posh stands for 'Port Out, Starboard Home' — the shady side of ships to India.
myth.truth: False. No evidence of the acronym exists; it's a later invention.

words.def: genuine, free from pretence
words.story: A charming tale says dishonest sculptors hid cracks with wax, so honest work was 'sine cera', without wax. Lovely — but invented. Latin sincerus simply meant clean or pure.
words.example: Please accept my sincere apologies.

myth.claim: Sincere comes from Latin 'sine cera', 'without wax', as in flawless sculpture.
myth.truth: False. It's from Latin sincerus, 'pure, unmixed'.

words.def: newly received information about recent events
words.story: News is just 'new' with a plural -s: new things, modelled on French nouvelles. People once said 'these news are good'.
words.example: Have you heard the news?

myth.claim: News is an acronym of North, East, West, South.
myth.truth: False. It's the plural of 'new' — 'new things'.

words.def: a game played by hitting a small ball into holes with clubs
words.story: The first record of golf is a 1457 Scottish law banning it because it distracted men from archery practice. The name most likely comes from a Dutch word for a club.
words.example: He spent Sunday playing golf.

myth.claim: Golf stands for 'Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden'.
myth.truth: False. It's recorded in 1457, long before acronyms; probably from Dutch kolf, 'club'.

words.def: a small extra sum of money given for good service
words.story: Tip began as underworld slang for handing something over. Acronym origins are almost always a giveaway: they were rare in English before the 20th century.
words.example: We left a generous tip for the waiter.

words.def: an outdoor meal

journey.gloss: a meal where each guest brings food

words.story: A widely shared claim gives picnic a racist origin story. It has none: it comes from 17th-century French pique-nique, a shared meal — recorded long before the events it's linked to.
words.example: We spread a blanket for a picnic by the river.

myth.claim: Picnic comes from racist gatherings in the American South.
myth.truth: False. It's from 1690s French pique-nique, a shared meal.

words.def: all right; acceptable

journey.gloss: joke abbreviation of 'oll korrect' in a Boston paper
Old Kinderhook clubs back Van Buren for president
the most widely used word on Earth

words.story: In 1839 Boston newspapers were mad for joke abbreviations of misspellings. Most died, but 'oll korrect' got a boost from President Van Buren's 'Old Kinderhook' campaign. Linguist Allen Walker Read proved it in the 1960s.
words.example: Is it OK if I sit here?

myth.claim: OK comes from the Choctaw word 'okeh'.
myth.truth: False. It's an 1839 joke abbreviation for 'oll korrect'.

words.def: the choice cut of beef from the upper loin
words.story: Legend says a king so loved the beef that he knighted it 'Sir Loin'. The story is so good it changed the spelling — but the word is plain French sur, 'above', the loin.
words.example: He ordered the sirloin, medium rare.

myth.claim: A king knighted a joint of beef, dubbing it 'Sir Loin'.
myth.truth: False. It's French surloigne, 'above the loin'.

words.def: a pear-shaped fruit with creamy green flesh
words.story: The Aztec word for the fruit, āhuacatl, also served as slang for testicles — they hang in pairs. Spanish speakers reshaped it into avocado, which already meant 'lawyer'.
words.example: She mashed an avocado onto her toast.

words.def: a sweet food made from roasted cacao seeds

journey.gloss: a drink; later the solid sweet

words.story: For its first centuries chocolate was a drink — bitter, frothy, often spiced with chilli. Scholars still argue about its exact Nahuatl form: an honest open case.
words.example: He hid the last bar of chocolate.

words.def: a red, juicy fruit eaten as a vegetable
words.story: English first borrowed it as tomate, like Spanish. It was later reshaped to rhyme with potato — itself from Taíno batata.
words.example: The tomatoes ripened on the windowsill.

words.def: a wealthy, powerful businessperson

journey.gloss: title used for the shogun with foreigners
the shogun; nickname for Abraham Lincoln

words.story: Japan's shogun was styled 'taikun' in dealings with foreign diplomats. Lincoln's secretaries jokingly called their boss 'the Tycoon', and the title later passed to the barons of business.
words.example: The shipping tycoon owned three islands.

words.def: a tomato sauce
words.story: Ketchup began as a fermented fish sauce in southern China. British sailors brought the idea home and tried it with mushrooms, walnuts and oysters before tomatoes won.
words.example: Pass the ketchup, please.

words.def: in a frenzied, out-of-control way (usually 'run amok')

journey.gloss: to rush about in a frenzy

words.story: European traders in Southeast Asia described warriors who charged in a fearless frenzy. Today it's mostly toddlers and puppies who run amok.
words.example: The goats ran amok in the vegetable garden.

words.def: a machine that can carry out complex actions automatically

journey.gloss: an artificial worker, in Karel Čapek's play R.U.R.

words.story: Writer Karel Čapek needed a name for the artificial workers in his play; his brother Josef suggested 'roboti', from robota, drudgery. German Arbeit, 'work', is a distant cousin.
words.example: A robot vacuum bumped into my foot.

words.def: remote, rough or isolated country
words.story: American soldiers in the Philippines picked up bundok, 'mountain', for the wild interior. It came home as boondocks — any place far from civilisation.
words.example: They bought a cabin out in the boondocks.

words.def: (of a word) very long; given to using long words
words.lit: a foot and a half long

journey.gloss: a foot and a half long

words.story: The Roman poet Horace advised writers to avoid 'words a foot and a half long'. The word for long words is, of course, itself a very long word.
words.example: His sesquipedalian prose needed a dictionary at hand.

words.def: the act of throwing someone out of a window

journey.gloss: coined after the Defenestration of Prague

words.story: In 1618 Protestant nobles in Prague threw two imperial officials and a secretary out of a castle window. All three survived. The event helped trigger the Thirty Years' War — and gave us this gloriously specific word.
words.example: He joked about the defenestration of his old laptop.

words.def: (of a sound or voice) sweet and smooth
words.story: A mellifluous voice pours like honey. The same honey root hides in molasses ('honey-like') and even mildew — Old English for 'honeydew'.
words.example: The narrator had a deep, mellifluous voice.

words.def: looking or sounding sad and dismal
words.story: Lugubrious things are fit for a funeral. Today it's often used playfully, for a basset hound's face or a cello's lament.
words.example: The basset hound gave us a lugubrious look.

words.def: lacking courage; timid
words.story: Its opposite is magnanimous — 'great-souled'. One spirit is tiny, the other huge. Animal and animate share that anim-, the breath of life.
words.example: The pusillanimous committee postponed the decision again.

words.def: the most perfect example of something
words.story: Ancient thinkers counted four elements — earth, water, air, fire — plus a fifth, the aether, from which the stars were made. Alchemists hunted for it. It became a word for the purest form of anything.
words.example: The cottage was the quintessence of cosiness.

words.def: a soft whispering or rustling sound
words.story: Say it slowly — susurrus — and you hear it. It's onomatopoeia: the word whispers what it means, like leaves in a breeze.
words.example: A susurrus of voices filled the gallery.

words.def: the warmth of the sun in winter
words.story: A word almost no one used for 400 years, now rescued by word-lovers. Despite appearances, apricot is no relation — it's from Latin praecoquum, 'early-ripening'.
words.example: We sat on the bench, soaking up the apricity.
